items.content_html:
i had a look at @zowoq's PR https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/522904/changes and realized that we automatically depend on qemu only if we actually configure VMs in a test instead of only containers. This dependency comes in automatically because we depend on VM runner scripts which themselves depend on qemu.
Because the test driver only runs those scripts and does not use qemu commands itself (all communication with qemu instances is via sockets), we don't need to define this dependency any longer.

(Unless i am missing out on something because i did not have enough sleep?)

items.content_html:
Reduces the number of dependencies for any user of services.qemuGuest by ~1715 requisites, including x265, SDL, ...etc. on headless systems.

More details (including how that number was calculated) can be found in each commit. Top level summary:

  • Add a pkg.qemu_ga target that builds the QEMU guest agent only as a minimal qemu build.- This makes it easier to reason with, apply overlays, or investigate the potential attack surface of this package.
  • Update the services.qemuGuest module to point to the new dedicated pkg
  • Added a release note that services.qemuGuest will no longer build documentation. That means anyone who uses services.qemuGuest will need to manually re-enable documentation afterwards or use the full qemu_kvm package like before.

  • Switched a Linux x86-64 qemu-kvm machine between the two module definitions, which happened without interruption

Add package for qemu-3dfx, a modified QEMU that allows GPU acceleration in Windows 9x/ME/2000/XP guests. There is also a set of packages of "guest wrappers" at qemu-3dfx.guestWrappers that are cross compiled for the guests, and an ISO file at qemu-3dfx.guestWrappers.iso that has an install script for moving all the wrappers to the right system directories. I tested the Half-Life: Uplink demo on Windows 98 SE (with win98-quickinstall), Windows ME (with win98-quickinstall), Windows 2000, and Windows XP, and everything seems to be working.

items.title: nixos/shadow: depend xauth on if a graphical desktop is enabled

items.content_html:
The qemu-vm.nix module gets a new mountHostNixStoreClosureOnly option.
The option mounts the user's host store with a lightweight projection (a "sub-store") of the VM closure, providing both great performance and correct security/privacy.

There are currently three ways to configure how the VM store is built:

  • mountHostNixStore (default): Mounts the store via 9p. Fast, but exposes the whole host store inside the VM.
  • useNixStoreImage: Builds an erofs image at runtime. Slower at runtime, but exposes only the closure of the VM.
  • useBootLoader: Builds a full qcow2 image with the closure inside it. Slowest at build time, exposes only the closure of the VM, duplicates the closure inside the qcow2 image, and thus into the store.

This PR proposes a fourth way, by combining both mountHostNixStore and (the new) mountHostNixStoreClosureOnly option. This method is fast, exposes only the closure of the VM inside the guest and does not store anything else into the store. In practice, this is implemented by wrapping the virtiofsd daemon through a light binary nix-substore over an unshared mount and user namespace. The binary reads the closure of the VM from a file built with pkgs.closureInfo and bind-mounts each store path into a tmpdir, which is the new so-called sub-store. The overhead consists only of O(n) calls to the mount syscall.

In an effort to standardize the way sharedDirectories are implemented, this PR moves all the sharedDirectories from 9p to virtiofsd. virtiofsd is "much faster" than 9p. However, virtiofsd does not implement the mapped-xattr and mapped-file security modes that 9p provides. In the current implementation, the only option for affected users would be to re-implement the shared directories themselves by using qemu.options and fileSystems.

If we cannot reach a consensus that the securityMode of 9p can be ignored in this re-implementation of the shared directories, I am open to supporting both 9p and virtiofsd and making the modifications required to support both.

As a side note, I would like to point out that, in the future, NixOS containers could be modified to also use the nix-substore binary (responsible for setting up the sub-stores) and expose only the closure of the container instead of the whole store.

I recommend that you review the PR commit by commit.

  • Allow nix-store to mount something else than /nix/store, just in case ;

items.content_html:
Using the target platform instead of the host allows us to build a targetted QEMU to the desired platform we want to test. For example, to test an ARM firmware, I can now call this to get a minimal QEMU:

pkgsCross.arm-embedded.buildPackages.qemu.override
{ targetCpuOnly = true }

Prior to this change, the QEMU would be built to execute x86-64 even if the specified target is ARM. This commit is the natural successor of the change I made to GDB [1].

[1] 28ded88

items.content_html:
Fixes: #489197

Qemu is moving to a new way of doing UEFI var storage:
Context:

  • https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/devel/uefi-vars.html
  • https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/edk2/-/blob/master/OvmfPkg/QEMU_PV_VARS.md
  • https://gitlab.com/kraxel/virt-firmware-rs/-/blob/main/varstore/README.md?ref_type=heads

This attempts to do so, but the build hangs on aarch64-linux.

I suspect this is because of the edk2-var-generator usage inside the derivation:

  1. It shouldn't be necessary, if we move to the json var storage.
  2. It's... vastly overkill. virt-firmware has a python script that can do this, seemingly without running qemu...

So this is a draft, because there's more work/consideration that needs to happen, hopefully from EDK2/OVMF/qemu maintainers.

items.content_html:
system.build.vm currently embeds startVM but does not expose it to the module system. This can make it considerably harder than necessary to customize system.build.vm with i.e. code to create and destroy additional resources on the host system, without vendoring all of startVM.

While introducing a custom system.build attribute might be a solution in some cases, much of the surrounding eco-system assumes VMs to be runnable via system.build.vm. Adhering to that convention allows one to run i.e. NixOS VM tests with a customized system.build.vm.

preVM/postVM attributes akin to pkgs.runInLinuxVM, etc were considered as an alternative, but would either provide suboptimal UX or require more code changes in a anready convoluted NixOS module.

This change should be a noop whenever one does not explicitly set system.build.vm to something other than the default. It supports the later by allowing e.g.:

 system.build.vm = lib.mkForce (
   hostPkgs.writeShellScriptBin "run-${config.system.name}-vm" ''
     ${createVmDisk}
     ${cfg.runner} $@
   ''
 );
